introduction: Titus Andronicus returns to Rome expecting public honour and rest after years of war. His victory brings captives into a city already divided over who should rule, and his insistence on Roman duty quickly entangles his family in further conflict. Tamora's loss as a mother gives her a cause for revenge, while Aaron turns opportunities at court into elaborate crimes. As violence attacks both bodies and the means of speaking, the struggle to discover and answer wrongdoing becomes inseparable from the collapse of lawful protection.

fullSynopsis.text: Titus Andronicus returns victorious to Rome with his surviving sons, his dead, and prisoners including Tamora, queen of the Goths. He permits his sons to sacrifice her eldest son Alarbus despite her appeal for mercy. Offered the imperial crown, Titus instead secures it for Saturninus, the late emperor's elder son. Saturninus chooses Titus's daughter Lavinia as empress, but her betrothed Bassianus claims her with her brothers' support. Titus kills his son Mutius for blocking his pursuit. Saturninus abandons Lavinia and marries Tamora, who publicly reconciles the factions while privately vowing to destroy the Andronici.

Tamora's lover Aaron directs her sons Chiron and Demetrius towards rape rather than rivalry over Lavinia. During the imperial hunt, Bassianus and Lavinia discover Tamora with Aaron. Tamora invents a threat against her life, and her sons murder Bassianus. Refusing Lavinia's plea for death instead of rape, Tamora leaves her to them. The brothers assault her and cut off her hands and tongue to prevent identification. Aaron meanwhile lures Titus's sons Quintus and Martius into the pit containing Bassianus's body. A forged letter and planted gold persuade Saturninus of their guilt. Marcus finds the mutilated Lavinia and brings her to her father.

Titus appeals vainly to Rome's judges for his condemned sons. Lucius, banished for attempting their rescue, joins his father and Marcus in grieving over Lavinia. Aaron falsely offers the emperor's pardon in exchange for a hand. Titus lets Aaron cut off his own, but receives it back with the two sons' severed heads. His grief turns into a vow of revenge, and he sends Lucius to raise an army among the Goths. At home, Titus struggles to interpret Lavinia's signs and preserve enough strength for vengeance; his response to Marcus killing a fly reveals how suffering and hatred distort his perception.

Lavinia uses the story of Philomela in Ovid to disclose the rape, then writes Chiron and Demetrius's names in sand with a staff guided by her mouth and the stumps of her arms. Titus sends the brothers weapons bearing pointed verses and later shoots petitions for justice towards the imperial court. Saturninus orders an innocent messenger hanged and fears news that Lucius leads the Goths. Meanwhile Tamora bears Aaron's child. Ordered to kill the baby, Aaron instead defends his son, kills the Nurse to conceal the birth, and plans to substitute another infant before fleeing with his own towards the Goths.

Captured with the baby, Aaron exchanges a full confession for Lucius's sworn promise to preserve and rear the child. He boasts of his crimes without repentance. Tamora, believing Titus mad, visits disguised as Revenge with Chiron and Demetrius as her attendants Rape and Murder. Titus recognizes them and pretends belief. He agrees to a banquet and secures the brothers' remaining with him while Tamora departs. His household binds them; Titus cuts their throats while Lavinia receives their blood. He prepares their remains as pies so that Tamora will consume her own sons, turning the story that helped expose Lavinia's suffering into a still more terrible revenge.

At the banquet, Titus asks Saturninus to endorse the example of a father killing his violated daughter, then kills Lavinia himself. He reveals that Tamora has eaten Chiron and Demetrius and stabs her. Saturninus kills Titus, and Lucius kills Saturninus. Marcus and Lucius explain the crimes and their reprisals to the assembled Romans, who acclaim Lucius as emperor. After mourning Titus with his young son, Lucius sentences Aaron to be buried breast-deep and starved, forbidding anyone to help him. Aaron remains defiant. Lucius orders honourable burial for Saturninus, Titus and Lavinia but denies Tamora funeral rites, consigning her body to beasts and birds. His hope to heal Rome follows a settlement still expressed through exclusion and punitive violence.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Rome's disputed succession coincides with Titus's return from war against the Goths. To honour his dead sons, he authorizes Alarbus's sacrifice despite Tamora's pleas. The people favour Titus for emperor, but he declines and advances Saturninus. The new emperor proposes to marry Lavinia, who is already promised to Bassianus. Marcus and Titus's sons support Bassianus's claim; Titus treats their resistance as treason and kills Mutius. Saturninus repudiates Lavinia and chooses Tamora instead. Titus's family persuades him to bury Mutius in the ancestral tomb. Tamora then obtains a public pardon and reconciliation while privately telling Saturninus that she will massacre the Andronici. A hunt is arranged for the next day.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Aaron celebrates his lover Tamora's rise and persuades Chiron and Demetrius to pursue Lavinia jointly by force. The imperial hunt provides their opportunity. Bassianus and Lavinia encounter Tamora with Aaron, and she falsely claims that they threatened her. Her sons kill Bassianus and, with her permission, carry Lavinia away despite her appeal for death rather than sexual assault. Aaron draws Quintus and Martius into the pit where Bassianus lies, then produces circumstances, a forged letter and hidden gold that make them appear murderers. Saturninus refuses Titus's offer of bail. Chiron and Demetrius leave Lavinia raped, tongueless and without hands; Marcus discovers her and leads her towards Titus.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Titus pleads for Quintus and Martius as they are taken to execution, but the judges pass without answering. Lucius reports his own banishment for trying to rescue them. Marcus brings Lavinia, and the family cannot yet identify her attackers. Aaron offers a false bargain: one of their hands will ransom the condemned men. Titus secretly has Aaron sever his hand before Marcus or Lucius can sacrifice theirs. The returned hand and the sons' heads expose the deception. Titus vows revenge and sends Lucius to the Goths for military support. At a family meal, he attempts to interpret Lavinia's signs and swings from pity for a killed fly to hatred when it is compared to Aaron.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Lavinia directs attention to Ovid's account of Philomela and, using a staff held with her mouth and guided by her arms, writes the names of her assailants. Titus sends Chiron and Demetrius weapons with verses that Aaron recognizes as accusation. Tamora gives birth to Aaron's son and orders the child's death, but Aaron protects him, kills the Nurse and plans a substitute baby before escaping. Titus and his relatives shoot appeals for justice into the court and send a messenger with pigeons and a letter. Saturninus orders the messenger's hanging. News of Lucius's Gothic army alarms him, and Tamora proposes to manipulate Titus into recalling his son.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Lucius's Goths capture Aaron and the baby. Aaron demands an oath securing his son's life, then recounts his part in the murders, rape, mutilations and false accusations. Tamora comes to Titus disguised as Revenge, accompanied by her sons as Rape and Murder. Recognizing them, Titus pretends to be deceived, retains the brothers and kills them, preparing their remains for Tamora's meal. At the banquet he kills Lavinia, exposes the pies and kills Tamora. Saturninus kills him and is killed by Lucius. The Romans choose Lucius emperor after hearing the family's account. Lucius sentences the unrepentant Aaron to starvation, orders family burials and refuses Tamora funeral honour.
